evaluation_inputs.system_description: An Event framework where the application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent. The Main module is part of the framework, and the Event Manager interacts directly with application handlers. It features an Event Queue and a base Handler component extended by standard and application-specific handlers.

phase_1_discovery.initial_documentation_status: Fully developed architecture with class diagrams, component descriptions, and defined component interactions.
evaluator_inquiry_questions: Can the components of the architecture be reused for future projects?
Can the framework be expanded in the future to accommodate a new application or new components?
Will the system handle any input given by the user and handle invalid input?
Is the architecture consistent in behavior?
Can any new application-specific functionality be added to the architecture?
Can the system be modified in short time and cost-effective manner?
Does the architecture perform its event-processing task properly?

hardware_view_description: System accepts input via Command Line Interface (CLI)
Single processor execution implied (sequential event processing)
runtime_constraints: Events must be dispatched in a First-Come-First-Served (FIFO) pattern
System must maintain an 'idle wait' state until input is received
Application logic is embedded within framework components

quantitative_model_parameters.performance_proxy: Number of components involved in a transaction
quantitative_model_parameters.transaction_speed: Qualitative (Slow due to high number of components involved)

questions: Does the system allow unauthorized access?
Does the architecture portray data confidentiality?
Does the architecture process any task in the fastest possible speed?

architectural_approaches.description: The system is organized around event handling, where the framework and application logic interact through events rather than a continuous control flow.

addressed_attributes.rationale: Event-based dispatch can centralize processing in the event path and support sequential handling of CLI input.
A single event-driven style provides a coherent model for how input is accepted and handled.

architectural_approaches.description: The architecture includes a single event queue that orders incoming events first-in, first-out before processing.

addressed_attributes.rationale: The queue provides a clear buffering mechanism for incoming events under sequential processing.
FIFO ordering helps preserve predictable handling order for queued events.

architectural_approaches.description: The system processes events on one processor in sequence, implying no concurrent execution of event handlers in the supplied evidence.

addressed_attributes.rationale: A single execution path reduces behavioral variation across component interactions.
Sequential execution matches the supplied performance proxy of component count per transaction, though it may also increase latency.

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Idle wait until input is received
architectural_approaches.description: The system remains idle until a CLI event arrives, rather than continuously processing in the absence of input.

addressed_attributes.rationale: Idle wait reduces unnecessary work when no events are available.
A stable idle state can simplify behavior when the system has no input to process.

architectural_approaches.approach_name: Embedded application logic inside framework components
architectural_approaches.description: The framework contains application-specific behavior and the Main module is part of the framework, creating a tight coupling between framework services and application handlers.

addressed_attributes.rationale: Embedded logic allows the framework to directly invoke application handlers during event processing.
Tight coupling can make changes more difficult, so this approach directly affects change impact and reuse.

scenario_reference.text: When a user enters a CLI command during normal operation, the system accepts it through the event queue and processes it sequentially on a single processor.

analysis_records.environment: Normal operation with CLI input and a single processor
analysis_records.stimulus: A user enters a CLI command
analysis_records.response_measure: Qualitative responsiveness of event handling under sequential processing; no numeric target is supplied
analysis_records.reasoning: The supplied architecture accepts CLI input through a single FIFO queue and handles events sequentially on one processor. This supports predictable event handling, but the qualitative performance proxy indicates slow transaction speed due to the number of components involved, so responsiveness may be limited by the length of the event-processing path.

risks.description: Responsiveness may be slow because event handling is sequential and the architecture already indicates slow transaction speed due to many components per transaction.
risks.rationale: The quantitative model explicitly states slow transaction speed and uses number of components involved in a transaction as the performance proxy.

non_risks.description: The FIFO queue gives a straightforward and deterministic path for accepting CLI commands.
non_risks.rationale: The architecture explicitly includes a FIFO event queue and sequential processing.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Number of components involved in a transaction

tradeoff_points.parameter: Sequential processing and tight framework/application coupling

scenario_reference.text: When multiple events arrive while the processor is busy, the system buffers them in FIFO order and processes them sequentially.

analysis_records.environment: Burst of queued events while the processor is active
analysis_records.stimulus: Multiple events arrive before the current event processing completes
analysis_records.response_measure: Queued events are handled in FIFO order with no evidence of parallel execution; no numeric latency target is supplied
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture directly supports buffering in a single FIFO queue and then processing events one at a time. This preserves arrival order, but waiting time can increase as the queue grows because there is only one processor and no evidence of concurrency or prioritization.

risks.description: Backlog and waiting time may grow when event arrival exceeds the sequential service rate.
risks.rationale: A single processor and FIFO queue imply one-at-a-time processing with no parallelism in the supplied evidence.

non_risks.description: Arrival order is preserved by the FIFO queue.
non_risks.rationale: FIFO is explicitly stated in the runtime constraints.

non_risks.description: No cross-thread ordering ambiguity is implied by the supplied single-processor model.
non_risks.rationale: The hardware view implies single processor execution and sequential processing.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Queue length at time of arrival
Arrival rate relative to processing time

scenario_reference.text: When no CLI input is present, the system remains in an idle wait state until input arrives.

analysis_records.response_measure: The system remains idle until input is received; wake-up latency is not quantified
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture explicitly states that the system maintains an idle wait state until input is received. This should avoid unnecessary active processing while idle, but the supplied inputs do not define the wake-up mechanism, so responsiveness on input arrival cannot be measured precisely.

risks.description: If the idle wait mechanism wakes slowly, user-perceived responsiveness may degrade when input arrives.
risks.rationale: The runtime constraint requires idle wait, but the implementation mechanism is not provided.

non_risks.description: Idle wait avoids continuous work when no events are present.
non_risks.rationale: This is directly supported by the supplied runtime constraint.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Polling versus blocking implementation of idle wait

scenario_reference.text: When event handling requires embedded application logic, the system completes dispatch and processing through the framework event path.

analysis_records.environment: Normal event handling with embedded application-specific behavior
analysis_records.stimulus: An event invokes application logic embedded in framework components
analysis_records.response_measure: Event processing completes through the framework path; exact timing is unknown
architectural_decisions: Embedded application logic inside framework components
analysis_records.reasoning: Because application logic is embedded within framework components and the Main module is part of the framework, dispatch and business logic are intertwined. This can reduce dispatch overhead by keeping the logic in one path, but it also makes the event path longer and more sensitive to code-path complexity.

risks.description: The embedded logic may dominate the hot path, making event-handling time sensitive to business logic complexity.
risks.rationale: The supplied architecture states that application logic is embedded within framework components and highly inter-dependent.

risks.description: The long and inter-dependent event path may be difficult to optimize for speed.
risks.rationale: High coupling typically increases change impact and makes optimization harder, but the supplied inputs do not quantify the effect.

non_risks.description: Keeping dispatch and application behavior in one path may reduce integration overhead.
non_risks.rationale: This is a reasonable inference from embedded logic, but it remains an inference rather than measured evidence.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of coupling between framework and application logic
Amount of work executed inline during dispatch

Base Handler extended by standard and application-specific handlers
analysis_records.reasoning: The presence of a base handler with standard and application-specific extensions suggests some extension mechanism exists. However, the supplied architecture is highly inter-dependent, so added functionality may require touching framework and application code together.

risks.description: Adding new application-specific functionality may require changes in tightly coupled framework code.
risks.rationale: The architecture explicitly states that application logic is embedded within framework components.

non_risks.description: A base Handler extended by standard and application-specific handlers provides some extension structure.
non_risks.rationale: This is directly stated in the system description.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of extension through handler inheritance versus framework modification

tradeoff_points.parameter: Tight integration of framework and application logic

architectural_decisions: Embedded application logic inside framework components
High inter-dependence between framework and application logic
analysis_records.reasoning: The architecture’s tight coupling suggests that even small changes may propagate across framework and application handlers. That makes rapid, low-cost modification uncertain and likely sensitive to the extent of embedded logic.

risks.description: Framework modifications may be expensive or slow because of tight coupling between framework and application logic.
risks.rationale: The system description explicitly states that application logic and framework are highly inter-dependent.

sensitivity_points.parameter: Degree of coupling between framework and application logic

tradeoff_points.parameter: Embedding application logic in framework components

scenario_reference.text: When a future project needs additional components or a new application, the framework can be expanded to support them.

analysis_records.response_measure: Expansion is possible without unsupported assumptions; no concrete capacity target is supplied

analysis_records.response_measure: Support for multiple applications is achievable; no concurrency or deployment target is supplied
